{{Use American English|date = April 2019}}
{{Short description|Solution of a state equation}}
{{more footnotes|date=January 2014}}

The '''state-transition equation''' is defined as the solution of the linear homogeneous state equation. The [[Linear time-invariant system|linear time-invariant]] state equation given by
<math display=block>\frac{d\mathbf{x}(t)}{dt} = \mathbf{Ax}(t) + \mathbf{Bu}(t) + \mathbf{Ew}(t), </math>
with state vector {{math|'''x'''}}, control vector {{math|'''u'''}}, vector {{math|'''w'''}} of additive disturbances, and fixed matrices {{math|'''A''', '''B''', '''E'''}} can be solved by using either the classical method of solving linear [[differential equations]] or the [[Laplace transform]] method. The Laplace transform solution is presented in the following equations.
The Laplace transform of the above equation yields 
<math display=block>s\mathbf{X}(s) - \mathbf{x}(0) = \mathbf{AX}(s) + \mathbf{BU}(s) + \mathbf{EW}(s) </math>
where {{math|'''x'''(0)}} denotes '''initial-state vector''' evaluated at {{math|1=''t'' = 0}}. Solving for {{math|'''X'''(s)}} gives
<math display=block> \mathbf{X}(s) = (s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})^{-1} \mathbf{x}(0) + (s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})^{-1}[\mathbf{BU}(s) + \mathbf{EW}(s)]. </math>
So, the state-transition equation can be obtained by taking [[inverse Laplace transform]] as 
<math display=block>\begin{align}
  x(t) &= \mathcal{L}^{-1} \Bigl\{ (s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})^{-1}\Bigr\} \mathbf{x}(0) + \mathcal{L}^{-1} \Bigl\{(s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})^{-1} [\mathbf{BU}(s) + \mathbf{EW}(s)] \Bigr\} \\
  &= \mathbf{\Phi}(t) \mathbf{x}(0) + \int_{0}^{t} \mathbf{\Phi}(t - \tau)[\mathbf{Bu}(\tau) + \mathbf{Ew}(\tau)]dt
\end{align}</math>
where {{math|'''&Phi;'''(''t'')}} is the [[state transition matrix]].

The state-transition equation as derived above is useful only when the initial time is defined to be at {{math|1=''t'' = 0}}. In the study of [[control system]]s, specially discrete-data control systems, it is often desirable to break up a state-transition process into a sequence of transitions, so a more flexible initial time must be chosen. Let the initial time be represented by {{math|''t''{{sub|0}}}} and the corresponding initial state by {{math|'''x'''(''t''{{sub|0}})}}, and assume that the input {{math|'''u'''(t)}} and the disturbance {{math|'''w'''(t)}} are applied at {{math|''t'' ≥ 0}}. 
Starting with the above equation by setting {{math|1=''t'' = ''t''{{sub|0}}}}, and solving for {{math|'''x'''(0)}}, we get 
<math display=block> \mathbf{x}(0) = \mathbf{\Phi}(-t_0) \mathbf{x}(t_0) - \mathbf{\Phi}(-t_0) \int_{0}^{t_0}\mathbf{\Phi}(t_0 - \tau)[\mathbf{Bu}(\tau) + \mathbf{Ew}(\tau)]d\tau.</math>
Once the state-transition equation is determined, the output vector can be expressed as a function of the initial state.
